subtitle: Learn the three kinds of search intent, why one query can mean several things, and how to treat intent labels as hypotheses you check.
outcomes: Name Broder's three intent classes and match example queries to them
Explain why many queries have more than one meaning, and which interpretations a very helpful result serves
Treat an intent label as a hypothesis and check it against the pages that rank
Describe the two spelling correction steps in the IR textbook, and what they do not tell you about search engines

lessons.title: Three kinds of intent
objectives: Define navigational, informational and transactional intent in Broder's words
Place example queries from Broder's paper in the right class
Tell Broder's classes apart from the practitioner label 'commercial investigation'

beats.caption: Andrei Broder's paper, A taxonomy of web search, sorts web queries by what the searcher intends to do.
Navigational: the immediate intent is to reach a particular site. Broder's example is Greyhound Bus, with greyhound.com as the probable target.
Informational: the intent is to acquire some information assumed to be present on one or more web pages. Broder notes many are extremely wide, like cars or San Francisco.
Transactional: the intent is to perform some web-mediated activity. The main categories include shopping and finding web-mediated services.
Commercial investigation is a fourth label practitioners often add. It is a working convention, not one of Broder's classes.

blocks.text: Broder's taxonomy groups web queries by the searcher's intent. Each class has a one-line definition in the paper.

items.name: Navigational
items.text: The immediate intent is to reach a particular site.

items.name: Informational
items.text: The intent is to acquire some information assumed to be present on one or more web pages.

items.name: Transactional
items.text: The intent is to perform some web-mediated activity.
Greyhound Bus, where the probable target is greyhound.com.
Broder says many informational queries are extremely wide, for instance cars or San Francisco.
Broder lists categories rather than single queries: shopping, finding various web-mediated services, and downloading files.

blocks.label: Good to know
blocks.text: You will often see a fourth label, commercial investigation. It is a working convention among practitioners, not part of Broder's saved definitions.

takeaways.text: Navigational means reaching a particular site.
Informational means acquiring information assumed to be on one or more web pages, and these queries can be extremely wide.
Transactional means performing a web-mediated activity, such as shopping.
Commercial investigation is a practitioner extension, not one of Broder's classes.

exercise.title: Sort your own keyword list
steps: Pick ten queries from a keyword list you work with.
Label each one navigational, informational or transactional.
Mark any query you could not place with a single label.
Ask Claude to sort the same list, then compare its labels with yours.
exercise.prompt_template: Here are ten search queries: [paste your queries]. For each one, say which of Broder's three classes (navigational, informational or transactional) fits best, and flag any query that could reasonably fit more than one.

reflection: Think of three searches you made this week. Which class would each fall into?
Were any of them hard to place in one class? What made them hard?
lessons.whats_next: Next, you'll see why the same words can mean different things to different searchers.

lessons.title: One query, several meanings
objectives: Explain why Google's rater guidelines say many queries have more than one meaning
Name the three kinds of interpretation a very helpful result serves
Explain what the rater guidelines are for, and what they are not

beats.caption: A searcher types mercury.
Google's rater guidelines point out that many queries have more than one meaning.
For mercury, the intent may be to learn about the planet or about the chemical element.
A very helpful result serves any dominant, common or reasonable minor interpretation.
The guidelines are for human raters. No single rating directly changes how a page ranks.

blocks.text: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines note that many queries have more than one meaning.

sections.heading: What a very helpful result serves

blocks.text: A very helpful result for any dominant, common or reasonable minor query interpretation/user intent.
blocks.cite: Google, Search Quality Rater General Guidelines

blocks.label: Keep in mind
blocks.text: The guidelines tell human raters how to judge results. Google says no single rating, or single rater, directly impacts how a page or site ranks.

takeaways.text: Many queries have more than one meaning.
The rater guidelines' example is mercury: the planet or the chemical element.
A very helpful result serves dominant, common or reasonable minor interpretations.
Rater guidelines guide human raters; no single rating directly changes rankings.

exercise.title: Map the meanings of a term
steps: Pick one short keyword your site targets.
Write down every meaning a searcher could have in mind.
Search for it and note which meanings the results serve.
Decide which meaning your page serves, and whether it is dominant, common or minor.
exercise.prompt_template: List the different things people might mean when they search for [keyword]. For each meaning, describe the kind of page that would help them.

reflection: Which of your target keywords could mean something other than what your page covers?
If your page serves a minor meaning, what more specific phrase would describe it better?
lessons.whats_next: Next, you'll see why any intent label, from a tool or from you, is a best guess.

lessons.title: Intent is a best guess
objectives: Explain what Broder says about inferring intent from a query
Treat a tool's intent label as a hypothesis
Check a label against the pages that currently rank

beats.caption: A keyword tool stamps the query mercury: 100% informational. This tool is hypothetical.
Broder wrote that inferring the user intent from the query is at best an inexact science, but usually a wild guess.
His taxonomy makes no assumption that intent can be inferred with any certitude from the query.
So the label becomes a hypothesis. Practitioners check it against the pages that rank before choosing a page type.

blocks.text: inferring the user intent from the query is at best an inexact science, but usually a wild guess
blocks.cite: Andrei Broder, A taxonomy of web search

blocks.text: Broder adds that the taxonomy makes no assumption that intent can be inferred with any certitude from the query.

sections.heading: What it means for intent labels

blocks.text: Keyword tools often give each query one intent label. Broder's caution applies to those labels too: they are guesses about what the searcher wants.

blocks.label: Practitioner routine
blocks.text: Label target queries with intent as a hypothesis. Then look at the pages that currently rank before you choose a page type. This routine is practitioner judgement, supported by Broder's caution.

items.text: next to each intent label in your keyword list.
especially queries with more than one plausible label.

takeaways.text: Broder calls inferring intent from a query at best an inexact science.
His taxonomy does not assume intent can be inferred with certitude.
Treat any intent label as a hypothesis and check it against what ranks.

exercise.title: Audit your intent labels
steps: Open a keyword list that already has intent labels.
Add a column called Confidence and mark each label high, medium or low.
For three low-confidence queries, search and note what kinds of pages rank.
Update the label where the results disagree with it.
exercise.prompt_template: Here are some search queries with intent labels from a keyword tool: [paste queries and labels]. For each, tell me how confident I should be in the label, and what I should look for in the search results to check it.

reflection: Which intent labels in your work have you treated as facts?
What would change in your content plan if one of them turned out wrong?
lessons.whats_next: Next, you'll look at a different step entirely: correcting how a query was typed.

lessons.title: Spelling correction
objectives: Explain why spelling correction is a separate step from reading intent
Define edit distance and its three operations
Describe how k-gram overlap finds candidate corrections
Explain why these textbook methods do not tell you how a given engine behaves

beats.caption: A user types carot but wants documents about carrot.
The IR textbook describes two steps: one based on edit distance, one based on k-gram overlap.
Edit distance is the minimum number of edits needed to turn one string into another. Insert one r, and carot becomes carrot.
The edits are insert, delete and replace a character. From cat to dog takes 3.
K-gram overlap finds words that share many short letter runs with the query. For bord, that includes aboard, boardroom and border.
Some candidates, like boardroom, are implausible. One method ranks the candidates by edit distance.

blocks.text: Working out what a searcher wants is a different job from fixing how they typed it. Introduction to Information Retrieval describes two steps for spelling correction: the first based on edit distance, the second based on k-gram overlap.
The edit distance between two strings is the minimum number of edit operations needed to turn one into the other.
The edit distance between cat and dog is 3: every letter is replaced.
A k-gram is a short run of k letters. The textbook uses a k-gram index to find vocabulary terms that have many k-grams in common with the query.

For the misspelling bord, this finds aboard, boardroom and border. Boardroom is an implausible correction, so one method takes these candidates and keeps the ones with a small edit distance to the query.

sections.heading: When every word is spelled right

blocks.text: Correcting each word on its own has limits. The textbook's example is flew form Heathrow: every word is a real word, so isolated-term correction would not catch the error.

blocks.label: Unconfirmed
blocks.text: These sources describe correction methods. They do not say how any particular search engine handles misspellings, so check live results before building pages around misspelled queries.

takeaways.text: Spelling correction is a separate step from reading intent.
Edit distance counts the fewest inserts, deletes and replacements between two strings.
K-gram overlap finds candidate words that share many letter runs with the query.
Correcting words one at a time misses errors like flew form Heathrow.
Textbook methods do not confirm what a given engine does.

exercise.title: Count the edits
steps: Work out the edit distance from jagwar to jaguar.
Work out the edit distance from bord to border.
Search for a common misspelling in your field and note whether the results match the corrected spelling.
exercise.prompt_template: Explain step by step how to calculate the edit distance between [word one] and [word two], using only insert, delete and replace.

reflection: Have you ever planned a page for a misspelled keyword? What did the search results show for it?
Why might a query with every word spelled correctly still be a typing mistake?
lessons.whats_next: Next, a short recap, then the course quiz.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Search intent gives you a useful working model, but not certainty. Broder's three classes describe what searchers try to do. Google's rater guidelines remind you that one query can mean several things. Spelling correction is a separate step, and the textbook methods do not confirm how any engine behaves.

multiple_choice_overrides.prompt: In Broder's taxonomy, what is the immediate intent of a navigational query?
options: B. Acquire information on web pages
D. Compare products before a purchase
multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: Broder defines the immediate intent of a navigational query as reaching a particular site. Wrong: 'Acquire information on web pages' - that is informational. 'Perform a web-mediated activity' - that is transactional. 'Compare products before a purchase' - commercial investigation is a practitioner label, not one of Broder's classes.

multiple_choice_overrides.prompt: Which statement matches what Broder says about inferring intent from a query?
options: A. It can be read with certainty from the query
B. It becomes exact once a query is long enough
C. It is at best an inexact science
D. It only matters for transactional queries
multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: Broder says inferring the user intent from the query is at best an inexact science, and the taxonomy does not assume intent can be inferred with certitude. Wrong: 'It can be read with certainty from the query' - Broder says the opposite. 'It becomes exact once a query is long enough' - no saved source says this. 'It only matters for transactional queries' - his caution covers every class.

multiple_choice_overrides.prompt: Why do Google's rater guidelines use 'mercury' as an example?
options: A. It has more than one meaning
B. It is a navigational query for one site
C. It is too short for raters to judge
D. It contains a common spelling error
multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: the guidelines say many queries have more than one meaning, and mercury may mean the planet or the chemical element. Wrong: 'It is a navigational query for one site' - the guidelines describe it as having several meanings. 'It is too short for raters to judge' - no saved source says this. 'It contains a common spelling error' - mercury is spelled correctly.

multiple_choice_overrides.prompt: A searcher types a company name to reach its official website. Which Broder class fits best?
multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: Broder defines navigational intent as reaching a particular site. Wrong: 'Informational' - that is acquiring information. 'Transactional' - that is performing a web-mediated activity. 'Commercial investigation' - a practitioner label, not one of Broder's classes. Intent from a query alone is inexact, so verify against what ranks.
